--- title: "Session 1 — Introduction to Data Science" subtitle: "Definition · What data looks like · Evolution · AI vs ML · Roles · The lifecycle · Applications" --- ::: {.callout-note} **This chapter answers one question: what is data science, and what does a data scientist actually do all day?** **Assumed knowledge:** none. This is the first chapter. You do not need Python yet — read the code in this chapter for the shape of it, not the detail. Every line is explained properly later. **The one idea to take away:** data science is a *sequence of steps*, not a single clever trick. This chapter walks the whole sequence once, quickly, so that the other fifteen chapters have somewhere to fit. ::: ## 🎯 Learning outcomes {#sec-s01-outcomes} By the end of this chapter you can: 1. Define data science in plain English, without jargon. 2. Tell structured, semi-structured and unstructured data apart, and give an example of each. 3. Explain how the field grew from hand calculation to machine learning. 4. Place AI, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI inside one another correctly. 5. Name the three main data jobs and say who you would hire for a given problem. 6. List the seven stages of the data science lifecycle in order. 7. Name four things you use every day that are built with data science. ## How this chapter is organised {#sec-s01-organisation} | Part | Question it answers | |---|---| | [A — What data science is](#sec-s01-a) | *What is it, and what is the raw material?* | | [B — Where it came from](#sec-s01-b) | *Why now? And how does AI fit in?* | | [C — Who does it, and how](#sec-s01-c) | *Which job, which steps, which problems?* | Parts A and B are ideas. Part C is the map you will follow for the rest of the course. # Part A — What data science is {#sec-s01-a} ## 1. Data science, defined {#sec-s01-topic-1} **Data science is the practice of turning recorded facts into decisions.** You start with facts somebody wrote down — sales, clicks, temperatures, photographs. You end with a decision somebody makes because of them — restock this item, block this payment, call this patient in early. Three things have to come together for that to work: | Ingredient | What it gives you | Without it | |---|---|---| | **Programming** | the ability to handle more rows than you could ever read | you are stuck with what fits on one screen | | **Mathematics** | a way to tell a real pattern from a coincidence | you find patterns in noise | | **Domain knowledge** | knowing what the numbers *mean* | you produce a correct answer to the wrong question | Data science exists because human judgement stops working at scale. You can eyeball a hundred rows. Nobody can eyeball ten million. ::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — the master chef"} **The everyday thing:** a chef in a busy kitchen. **The mapping:** - The **raw ingredients** delivered at the back door are your raw data. - The **knives and ovens** are your programming tools. - The **recipes** are your mathematical methods. - The **plated dish** is the decision somebody acts on. **Where it breaks down:** a chef uses ingredients up. Data can be used a thousand times and is still there afterwards. ::: ### Demo 1 — data science in seven lines Here is the entire field, small enough to fit on a screen. Ten shops, their advertising spend, and what they sold. The question: **if I spend ₹45,000 on advertising, what should I expect to sell?** ::: {#cell-fig-s01-tiny .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt advertising = np.array([10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 50, 55, 60]) # ₹ thousands sales = np.array([32, 41, 46, 59, 61, 72, 79, 94, 99, 108]) # ₹ thousands slope, intercept = np.polyfit(advertising, sales, 1) # find the best straight line predicted = slope * 45 + intercept # use it to answer the question plt.scatter(advertising, sales, label="shops we have data for") plt.plot(advertising, slope * advertising + intercept, color="red", label="the pattern") plt.scatter([45], [predicted], color="green", s=140, zorder=5, label="our prediction") plt.xlabel("Advertising spend (₹ thousands)") plt.ylabel("Sales (₹ thousands)") plt.legend() plt.show() print(f"Spend ₹45,000 and expect sales of about ₹{predicted*1000:,.0f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Ten shops. A line through them. One prediction.](session-01-introduction-to-data-science_files/figure-html/fig-s01-tiny-output-1.png){#fig-s01-tiny width=681 height=408} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Spend ₹45,000 and expect sales of about ₹85,646 ``` ::: ::: That is the whole shape of it: **data in, pattern found, question answered.** Everything else in this course is doing that more carefully, on messier data. ### ❓ Check yourself **Q1.** Which is the most accurate description of data science? - (a) Writing software applications for web browsers. - (b) **Turning recorded facts into decisions, using programming, mathematics and knowledge of the subject.** - (c) Reading customer emails to find complaints. - (d) Installing and maintaining servers. **Q2.** A model correctly predicts which patients will be readmitted to hospital, but the team did not realise the "discharge code" column is only filled in *after* a readmission is scheduled. Which ingredient was missing? - (a) Programming. - (b) Mathematics. - (c) **Domain knowledge.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"} **A1 — (b).** (a) is software engineering, (c) is manual research, (d) is IT administration. **A2 — (c).** The code ran and the maths was sound. Only somebody who knew the hospital's process would spot that the column contains the answer. ::: **We have said "data" a dozen times. It is worth being precise about what that word covers, because it is wider than a spreadsheet.** ## 2. The three kinds of data {#sec-s01-topic-2} **Data comes in three shapes, and the shape decides how much work you have to do before you can analyse it.** | Kind | What it looks like | Examples | Effort to analyse | |---|---|---|---| | **Structured** | rows and columns, every row the same shape | spreadsheets, CSV files, SQL tables | low | | **Semi-structured** | has labels, but rows can differ | JSON, XML, log files | medium | | **Unstructured** | no rows or labels at all | text, photographs, audio, video | high | Most of this course works with structured data, because that is where the ideas are clearest. The techniques for the other two are the same ideas with more preparation in front of them. ### Demo 2 — the same fact in three shapes One customer's order, written three ways. ::: {#5fc92ed0 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd import json # STRUCTURED — a table. Every row has exactly the same columns. structured = pd.DataFrame({ "order_id": [1, 2], "customer": ["Alice", "Bob"], "amount": [250.0, 90.0], }) print("STRUCTURED — always the same columns") print(structured) # SEMI-STRUCTURED — labelled, but the second record has a field the first does not. semi = [ {"order_id": 1, "customer": "Alice", "amount": 250.0}, {"order_id": 2, "customer": "Bob", "amount": 90.0, "gift_wrap": True}, ] print("\nSEMI-STRUCTURED — labelled, but the shape varies") print(json.dumps(semi, indent=2)) # UNSTRUCTURED — a human sentence. No labels at all. unstructured = "Alice ordered two books on Tuesday and paid 250 rupees." print("\nUNSTRUCTURED — the same facts, but nothing is labelled") print(unstructured) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` STRUCTURED — always the same columns order_id customer amount 0 1 Alice 250.0 1 2 Bob 90.0 SEMI-STRUCTURED — labelled, but the shape varies [ { "order_id": 1, "customer": "Alice", "amount": 250.0 }, { "order_id": 2, "customer": "Bob", "amount": 90.0, "gift_wrap": true } ] UNSTRUCTURED — the same facts, but nothing is labelled Alice ordered two books on Tuesday and paid 250 rupees. ``` ::: ::: Look at what changes. In the table, "what did Alice pay?" is one lookup. In the JSON it is still easy, but your code must cope with `gift_wrap` existing on some records and not others. In the sentence, the number `250` is just characters — a program has to be taught that it is money before it can add it up. ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Semi-structured data breaks code that assumes a fixed shape"} Loading the JSON above into a table gives Alice a `gift_wrap` value of `NaN` — "not recorded". Code that assumes every record has every field will crash or, worse, quietly skip records. **Check the shape of every record, not just the first one.** ::: ::: {#eabf90da .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # What happens when you force semi-structured data into a table: print(pd.DataFrame(semi)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` order_id customer amount gift_wrap 0 1 Alice 250.0 NaN 1 2 Bob 90.0 True ``` ::: ::: # Part B — Where it came from {#sec-s01-b} ## 3. How the field grew {#sec-s01-topic-3} **Data science did not appear suddenly. It is statistics, plus two things statistics never had: enormous amounts of data, and cheap computing.** | Era | Data available | The hard part | Typical method | |---|---|---|---| | **Statistics** (before ~2000) | small, carefully collected samples | collecting data at all | averages, hypothesis tests, done by hand | | **Big data** (~2000–2010) | huge, collected automatically | *storing and querying* it | databases, Hadoop, SQL | | **Machine learning** (~2010–now) | huge, and cheap to process | choosing what to learn | algorithms that find the pattern themselves | | **Generative AI** (~2020–now) | the whole internet | steering the output | very large models that produce text and images | The shift that matters: **early on, a human proposed the pattern and used data to test it. Now the machine proposes the pattern and the human tests it.** ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Newer is not better"} An average — a technique from the 1800s — solves a great many business problems faster and more reliably than a neural network. **Always try the simple method first**, and keep it as the score your complicated method has to beat. A model that cannot beat an average has not worked. ::: ### Demo 3 — the simple method is hard to beat Two ways to predict tomorrow's demand. The plain one: **the average of every past day.** The reactive one: **whatever happened yesterday.** Judge them over sixty days, not one — on a single day either can win by luck. ::: {#bbc5d22b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np np.random.seed(0) demand = 100 + np.random.normal(0, 12, size=400) # wobbles randomly around 100 avg_errors, yest_errors = [], [] for day in range(60, len(demand)): history = demand[:day] avg_errors.append(abs(demand[day] - history.mean())) # predict the running average yest_errors.append(abs(demand[day] - demand[day - 1])) # predict yesterday's value print(f"Predicting with the running average : average error {np.mean(avg_errors):5.2f}") print(f"Predicting with yesterday's value : average error {np.mean(yest_errors):5.2f}") print(f"\nThe average was better on {np.mean(np.array(avg_errors) < np.array(yest_errors)):.0%} of days.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Predicting with the running average : average error 9.57 Predicting with yesterday's value : average error 13.45 The average was better on 62% of days. ``` ::: ::: When data wobbles randomly around a stable level, **the plain average wins**, because yesterday's wobble carries no information about today. Notice that it does *not* win every day — it wins on average, which is the only sense in which one method beats another. **This is why a single comparison proves nothing, and why Session 11 exists.** ## 4. AI, machine learning, deep learning, generative AI {#sec-s01-topic-4} **These four words are used interchangeably in the news. They are not the same thing. They sit inside one another.** ```{mermaid} flowchart TB AI["Artificial Intelligence
any machine doing something that
would need human intelligence"] ML["Machine Learning
the machine learns the rules from data
instead of being given them"] DL["Deep Learning
machine learning using neural networks
with many layers"] GEN["Generative AI
deep learning that produces new
text, images, audio or code"] AI --> ML --> DL --> GEN ``` The useful distinction is **who writes the rule**: | | Who writes the rule | Example | |---|---|---| | Ordinary programming | you do | *"if amount > 10000, flag it"* | | Machine learning | the machine, from examples | show it 50,000 past frauds; it works out what fraud looks like | **Data science is the wider job.** It includes machine learning, but it also includes collecting the data, cleaning it, exploring it, and explaining the result to somebody who has to act on it. In most real projects the machine learning is the *smallest* part. ### ❓ Check yourself **Q3.** A shop's till software prints a discount when the total is over ₹5,000. Is this machine learning? - (a) Yes, because a computer decided. - (b) **No — a human wrote the rule. The machine learned nothing.** - (c) Yes, because it uses customer data. **Q4.** Which statement is true? - (a) Machine learning includes artificial intelligence. - (b) **Deep learning is one kind of machine learning.** - (c) Generative AI and data science are the same thing. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"} **A3 — (b).** The rule was written by a person and never changes. Machine learning would be the till working out *for itself*, from past receipts, which customers respond to a discount. **A4 — (b).** AI is the widest circle; machine learning sits inside it; deep learning sits inside machine learning; generative AI sits inside deep learning. ::: # Part C — Who does it, and how {#sec-s01-c} ## 5. The three data jobs {#sec-s01-topic-5} **Building the pipes, reading the past, and predicting the future are three different jobs.** Most teams split them because the skills barely overlap. | Role | Owns | Main tools | Delivers | |---|---|---|---| | **Data engineer** | getting data in, reliably | SQL, Python, cloud services | a clean, fast, trustworthy table | | **Data analyst** | explaining what happened | SQL, spreadsheets, dashboards | a report somebody reads | | **Data scientist** | predicting what will happen | Python, scikit-learn | a model somebody uses | ::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — the car factory"} - The **data engineer** builds the assembly line and makes sure steel arrives on time. - The **data analyst** counts the cars coming off it and reports how many had defects. - The **data scientist** works out which factory settings *cause* defects, so next month's run has fewer. ::: Two more titles you will meet: the **machine learning engineer**, who takes a working model and makes it survive real traffic, and the **BI developer**, who builds the dashboards an analyst designs. ### ❓ Check yourself **Q5.** Terabytes of messy log files sit on ten different servers, and nobody can query them. Who do you hire first? - (a) Data scientist. - (b) **Data engineer.** - (c) Data analyst. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"} **A5 — (b).** Until the data is somewhere queryable, the other two have nothing to work with. This is the most common sequencing mistake real teams make. ::: ## 6. The data science lifecycle {#sec-s01-topic-6} **Every data science project runs through the same seven stages, in the same order. This course is those seven stages, one at a time.** | # | Stage | The question | Covered in | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | **Problem definition** | What decision will this change? | this chapter, and Session 16 | | 2 | **Data collection** | Where do the facts live? | Session 2 | | 3 | **Cleaning and preparation** | What is wrong with them? | Sessions 3–6 | | 4 | **Exploration** | What is actually in here? | Sessions 7–8 | | 5 | **Modelling** | What pattern can be learned? | Sessions 9–10 | | 6 | **Evaluation** | Is the pattern real? | Session 11 | | 7 | **Deployment** | How does somebody use it? | Session 12 | ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Stage 3 is most of the work"} Beginners expect modelling to take the longest. In practice, **collecting and cleaning the data takes most of a project**, and modelling is often an afternoon. This is why Sessions 2 to 8 — seven of sixteen — are about data rather than about algorithms. ::: ### Demo 4 — all seven stages in one cell This is the entire lifecycle, on tiny data, so you can see the whole shape before we slow down and do each stage properly. **You are not expected to follow the detail yet.** ::: {#99725d7e .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd import numpy as np from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression # STAGE 1 — PROBLEM: predict a flat's monthly rent from its size and its age. # STAGE 2 — COLLECT flats = pd.DataFrame({ "sqft": [500, 750, 1000, 1200, 1500, 900, 1100, np.nan, 1300, 600], "age_yrs": [10, 5, 2, 8, 1, 15, 3, 6, 4, 20], "rent": [9000, 14000, 20000, 21000, 28000, 15000, 21000, 16000, 25000, 10000], }) print(f"Stage 2 — collected {len(flats)} flats") # STAGE 3 — CLEAN: one flat has no recorded size. Fill it with the middle value. flats["sqft"] = flats["sqft"].fillna(flats["sqft"].median()) print(f"Stage 3 — cleaned; missing sizes remaining: {flats['sqft'].isna().sum()}") # STAGE 4 — EXPLORE: which column moves with rent? print("\nStage 4 — how strongly each column tracks rent:") print(flats.corr()["rent"].drop("rent").round(2)) # STAGE 5 — MODEL X = flats[["sqft", "age_yrs"]] y = flats["rent"] model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y) print(f"\nStage 5 — model trained. Rent rises about " f"₹{model.coef_[0]:.0f} for each extra square foot.") # STAGE 6 — EVALUATE: how close are its answers on flats it has seen? print(f"Stage 6 — it explains {model.score(X, y):.1%} of the variation in rent") # STAGE 7 — DEPLOY: wrap it so somebody else can ask it a question. def estimate_rent(sqft, age_yrs): row = pd.DataFrame({"sqft": [sqft], "age_yrs": [age_yrs]}) return model.predict(row)[0] print(f"\nStage 7 — a 1000 sqft, 5-year-old flat: ₹{estimate_rent(1000, 5):,.0f} per month") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Stage 2 — collected 10 flats Stage 3 — cleaned; missing sizes remaining: 0 Stage 4 — how strongly each column tracks rent: sqft 0.98 age_yrs -0.72 Name: rent, dtype: float64 Stage 5 — model trained. Rent rises about ₹18 for each extra square foot. Stage 6 — it explains 97.4% of the variation in rent Stage 7 — a 1000 sqft, 5-year-old flat: ₹18,527 per month ``` ::: ::: Every stage above is one line here and one *chapter* later. Session 3 spends a whole chapter on that single `fillna`, because there are six ways to do it and choosing wrongly changes the answer. ## 7. What it is used for {#sec-s01-topic-7} **Any process that currently relies on somebody guessing can usually be improved by finding the pattern in what happened before.** | Application | What it predicts | You meet it in | |---|---|---| | **Recommendations** | what you will watch or buy next | Netflix, Amazon, Spotify | | **Dynamic pricing** | what you will pay | airlines, ride-hailing, hotels | | **Fraud detection** | whether this payment is genuine | your bank, every card swipe | | **Medical diagnostics** | whether this scan shows disease | radiology departments | | **Demand forecasting** | how much stock to order | every large retailer | | **Predictive maintenance** | which machine fails next | factories, airlines, railways | | **Route optimisation** | how long the journey takes | maps, delivery firms | | **Credit scoring** | whether a loan is repaid | lenders — and Sessions 9 and 12 | ### Demo 5 — a recommendation, from scratch Recommendation engines sound complicated. The simplest useful one is a single idea: **find the person most like you, and suggest what they liked that you have not seen.** ::: {#561cf496 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd # Rows are viewers, columns are films, values are ratings out of 5 (0 = not watched). ratings = pd.DataFrame( [[5, 4, 0, 5, 1], [4, 5, 1, 4, 1], [1, 0, 5, 1, 4], [5, 4, 1, 0, 2]], index=["Asha", "Brij", "Chan", "You"], columns=["Action1", "Action2", "Romance1", "Action3", "Romance2"], ) print(ratings) # How similar is each viewer to you? Count agreement across the films you have both seen. you = ratings.loc["You"] others = ratings.drop("You") similarity = others.apply(lambda person: (person * you).sum(), axis=1) print("\nSimilarity to you:") print(similarity.sort_values(ascending=False)) closest = similarity.idxmax() unseen = ratings.columns[you == 0] print(f"\nYour closest match is {closest}.") for film in unseen: print(f" {closest} rated {film}: {ratings.loc[closest, film]}/5 → recommended") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Action1 Action2 Romance1 Action3 Romance2 Asha 5 4 0 5 1 Brij 4 5 1 4 1 Chan 1 0 5 1 4 You 5 4 1 0 2 Similarity to you: Asha 43 Brij 43 Chan 18 dtype: int64 Your closest match is Asha. Asha rated Action3: 5/5 → recommended ``` ::: ::: Real systems do this across millions of users with far better similarity measures, but the idea on screen is the idea they use. ### Demo 6 — what you will be able to build By Session 12 you will train a model and put it behind a web page. Here is the kind of output that page will show: history, a prediction, and an honest band around it. ::: {#cell-fig-s01-forecast .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt np.random.seed(42) days = np.arange(1, 101) price = 50 + days * 0.5 + np.random.normal(0, 5, size=100) future = np.arange(101, 121) slope, intercept = np.polyfit(days, price, 1) forecast = slope * future + intercept spread = price.std() plt.plot(days, price, label="What happened", alpha=0.75) plt.plot(future, forecast, "r--", lw=2, label="What we predict") plt.fill_between(future, forecast - 2*spread, forecast + 2*spread, color="red", alpha=0.15, label="Range we are fairly sure about") plt.xlabel("Day") plt.ylabel("Price") plt.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![History in blue, prediction in red, uncertainty shaded. The shaded band is the honest part.](session-01-introduction-to-data-science_files/figure-html/fig-s01-forecast-output-1.png){#fig-s01-forecast width=681 height=408} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ A prediction without a range is a guess in a suit"} The dashed red line looks authoritative. The shaded band is the honest part — it says how wrong the line could reasonably be. **A number reported without its uncertainty invites a decision it cannot support.** Session 11 is about measuring that band. ::: # 🎯 Tasks {#sec-s01-tasks} ::: {.callout-note title="✏️ Do these before Session 2"} **Task 1 — Classify some data.** For each of these, say whether it is structured, semi-structured or unstructured: a supermarket receipt photographed on your phone; the same receipt typed into a spreadsheet; your phone's location history export; a podcast episode; a weather API response. **Task 2 — Pick the role.** For a company you know well, write one specific project for a data engineer, one for a data analyst, and one for a data scientist. **Task 3 — Change a prediction.** In Demo 1, change the advertising figure from `45` to `80` and run the cell. The prediction goes up. Now look at the data: the largest shop we actually observed spent 60. **Write one sentence on why the prediction for 80 should be trusted less than the prediction for 45.** ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"} **Task 1.** Photographed receipt — unstructured (an image). Typed into a spreadsheet — structured. Location history export — semi-structured (usually JSON). Podcast — unstructured (audio). Weather API response — semi-structured (JSON). **Task 3.** 45 sits inside the range we observed (10 to 60), so the line is supported by nearby real shops. 80 is beyond every shop in the data — the line has been *extended* into territory where we have no evidence the relationship still holds. Predicting outside the observed range is called **extrapolation**, and it is where models fail most confidently. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="✅ Before you move on"} - [ ] I can define data science in one sentence without using the word "data science" - [ ] I can give an example of structured, semi-structured and unstructured data - [ ] I can draw AI, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI as nested circles - [ ] I can name the seven lifecycle stages in order - [ ] **Easiest thing to forget:** stages 2 and 3 — collecting and cleaning — take most of a real project. The modelling is usually the quick part. :::
